books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, 1835

stimulus.text:
Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835), on the peoples of the United States:

“Three races naturally distinct, and I might almost say hostile to each other, are discoverable among them at the first glance. ... fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.”

“As soon as it is admitted that the whites and the emancipated blacks are placed upon the same territory in the situation of two alien communities, it will readily be understood that there are but two alternatives for the future; the negroes and the whites must either wholly part or wholly mingle.”

“I do not imagine that the white and black races will ever live in any country upon an equal footing.”

Background: Tocqueville, a French visitor, traveled in the United States in 1831–1832 and published Democracy in America in 1835.
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (Reeve translation, 1835), public domain, as printed on Wikisource.

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1, ch. 18 (1835), public domain
stem: Tocqueville wrote that freed Black people and whites stood as 'two alien communities.' What did he think that meant for the future?

options.text: Slavery would end quietly on its own
options.misconception: Tocqueville describes a hard choice ahead, not a quiet ending.

options.text: The races would soon forget their differences
options.misconception: He doubted the races would ever live on an equal footing.

options.text: The federal government would force the races to mix together
options.misconception: Tocqueville names no government power that could force mixing.

options.text: The races must part or mix, and he doubted equal footing

rationales.A: Nothing in the passage promises a quiet end. Tocqueville sees a choice between parting and mixing, both hard.
rationales.B: He says the opposite. He does not imagine the races ever living on an equal footing.
rationales.C: The passage gives no such power to the government. The choice he names is between the peoples themselves.
rationales.D: Only two futures are open, parting or mixing, and he doubts equal footing will ever come.
rationales.general:
1. Read the choice Tocqueville offers. Two peoples on one territory must either wholly part or wholly mingle.
2. Add his doubt. He does not imagine the white and black races ever living on an equal footing.
3. Name the future he expects. Separation or mixing, with equality unlikely, is a hard road either way.
Remember: when a writer lists only two futures, both of them are usually hard.
